summary: Natamycin (Natacyn 5% ophthalmic suspension) is a polyene antifungal for fungal blepharitis, conjunctivitis and keratitis caused by susceptible organisms, including Fusarium solani keratitis. It binds fungal cell-membrane sterols, is predominantly fungicidal, and is essentially not absorbed systemically. For keratitis, dosing starts hourly or every 2 hours and is tapered over 14-21 days guided by clinical response and corneal scraping smear/culture. It is the standard first-line topical agent for filamentous fungal keratitis.

moa: Natamycin is a tetraene polyene antibiotic derived from Streptomyces natalensis. It binds the sterol moiety of the fungal cell membrane, forming a polyene-sterol complex that alters membrane permeability and causes depletion of essential intracellular constituents, producing a predominantly fungicidal effect. It is active against yeasts and filamentous fungi (Candida, Aspergillus, Cephalosporium, Fusarium, Penicillium) but not against bacteria.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to natamycin or any component of the formulation
relative: Failure to improve after a week may indicate a resistant organism - reassess rather than continue blindly
monitor: Repeat corneal scraping/culture if not responding

preg: Animal reproduction studies have not been conducted and it is unknown whether topical natamycin can cause fetal harm. Given negligible systemic absorption, risk is expected to be low; use during pregnancy only if clearly needed.
lact: It is not known whether natamycin is excreted in human milk, but systemic absorption after topical ocular use is negligible, so it is generally considered compatible with breastfeeding.
renal: No dosage adjustment; systemic absorption is negligible after topical ocular administration.
hepatic: No dosage adjustment; systemic absorption is negligible after topical ocular administration.

minor: No clinically significant systemic drug interactions are expected given negligible absorption

rare: Chest pain, dyspnea or paresthesia (rare post-marketing reports)
emergency: Severe allergic reaction with swelling or breathing difficulty

missed: If a dose is missed, instill it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and resume the regular schedule - do not use extra drops to make up.
overdose: Topical ocular overdose or accidental ingestion is unlikely to cause systemic toxicity because natamycin is very poorly absorbed from the eye and gastrointestinal tract. If excess is instilled, flush the eye with water; manage any local irritation symptomatically.
